newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Rock 'n roll, pan pipes, grey uniforms in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Rock 'n roll, pan pipes, grey uniforms in Belgrade.

text.p: Heavy metal music resounded through the streets of downtown Belgrade on Tuesday as hundreds of grim-faced paramilitary police in grey uniforms and helmets marched into position.
They formed a wedge-shaped blocking position, facing outwards and lining the edge of two broad avenues on the 77th day of pro-democracy protests.

Companies of anti-riot police four abreast were held in reserve, clutching perspex shields, automatic pistols on their belts along with with gasmasks and three-foot (one metre) long U.S.-style billie clubs.

They were large men, mostly, their heavy body armour helping to create the impression of brute strength. Most looked bored, and tried to ignore the taunts of people who stepped forward to challenge or curse them.

Initially, the sight of the grey lines moving towards Republic Square, the venue of most of the daily rallies, sent a frisson of nervous excitement through the crowd of opposition demonstrators, students and sightseers.
Despite some of the worst violence seen on Belgrade streets in years when police forcibly cleared demonstrators on Sunday night, leaving at least 100 people injured, there were no signs of panic.
People still lounged over coffee and croissants behind plate glass windows, mothers still tugged reluctant children in and out of shops and young lovers sat on benches holding hands.

But as the ranks formed, the police drew jeers and whistles from old and young alike, from students in jeans sporting faculty badges to businessmen with leather briefcases and tall blondes in puffer jackets and thigh-length boots.
Crowds surged along the pavements, moving towards Republic Square where opposition banners and flags fluttered in the chilly wind. One elderly woman held up a large poster of a saint.
Another man gestured rudely at the police and shouted "Ustashe" - a reference to the Croatian fascist regime set up in Zagreb by the Nazis in World War Two.
A grizzled old man waved his fist in front of a policeman's face and launched into a stream of invective. The policeman looked faintly embarrassed, but did not respond.
In the centre of the police square stood a tall officer with his beret set at a rakish angle.

With two gold bars and three stars on his epaulettes, he was clearly in command, and looked as if he enjoyed holding centre stage. He muttered into a hand-held radio and seemed unconcerned by the rock music blasting out from speakers above his head from the fourth storey of an office block.
Yards away in a pedestrian precinct, a group of six Peruvian pan pipers danced in a circle, woolly hats on their heads, their craftwork and jewellery carefully laid out on the paving stones for sale.
Popcorn and peanut sellers were doing a roaring trade.
Child beggars, muddy-faced and dressed in rags also established themselves on the street to reap what benefits they could from the 30,000-strong crowd.
Shop assistants emerged from up-market boutiques to blow large, technicolour whistles. Copies of a new independent newspaper, Democracy, were selling fast.

Addressing Tuesday's rally, opposition politician Vuk Draskovic spoke of the unbending spirit of Belgraders. Property dealers, he said, were now advertising central apartments with a good view of police lines.
"Not even the dumb blondes, let alone us, trust (Serbian President Slobodan) Milosevic any more," said one habitual rally-goer.
